summary: Specifies how to use EAP-TLS with TLS 1.3 while staying backwards compatible with existing EAP-TLS implementations. TLS 1.3 brings better security, privacy, and lower latency. Compared with older versions, EAP-TLS 1.3 always provides forward secrecy, does not disclose the peer identity, and requires revocation checking. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Network logins that use certificates now follow the newer, safer rules, so your ID stays private and old recordings cannot be unlocked later.

subtitle: How certificate-based network logins (EAP-TLS) use TLS 1.3 for forward secrecy, hidden identities and mandatory revocation checks.

tldr.problem: EAP-TLS, the certificate-based login method used on Wi-Fi and other 802.1X networks, was written for TLS 1.0 and 1.1. TLS 1.3 changes the handshake, key schedule, resumption and privacy handling so much that much of the older text no longer applies.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9190 says how EAP-TLS runs over TLS 1.3. The TLS handshake is carried inside EAP packets, keys come from the TLS exporter, a one-byte application data value 0x00 signals protected success, and resumption uses TLS 1.3 tickets.
tldr.outcome: EAP-TLS 1.3 always gives forward secrecy, never discloses the peer identity, and requires revocation checking. The RFC updates RFC 5216 and is itself updated by RFC 9965.

today: RFC 9190 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5216, and the unit metadata shows it is itself updated by RFC 9965. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why EAP-TLS Needed a TLS 1.3 Update
sections.content:
The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) is a standard way to plug different login methods into a network. EAP-TLS is the method that does certificate-based mutual authentication by running the TLS handshake inside EAP packets. The RFC notes it is widely supported in Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11) and MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) networks using IEEE 802.1X, and is the default certificate-based method in 3GPP 5G.

The original specification, RFC 5216, references TLS 1.0 and 1.1, which are now formally deprecated. TLS 1.3 remodels the handshake: different message flow, key schedule, cipher suites, resumption and privacy protection. Parts of RFC 5216 therefore do not apply to it.

RFC 9190 only describes the differences from RFC 5216. When an older TLS version is negotiated, RFC 5216 still applies. Implementations MUST limit the maximum TLS version they use to 1.3 unless an administrator explicitly enables later versions. Other TLS-based EAP methods are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rulebook for showing your digital ID to a network was written for old locks. This new rulebook says how to use the new, stronger lock without changing everything else.

sections.title: The Conversation: Handshake, Tickets and Resumption
sections.content:
The EAP server asks for an identity, then sends a TLS Start. The peer (the TLS client) answers with a ClientHello, and the TLS handshake continues inside EAP-Request and EAP-Response packets. The server MUST authenticate with a certificate and SHOULD require the peer to do so too. Pre-Shared Key (PSK) authentication SHALL NOT be used except for resumption.

When the server has processed the client Finished message and sent its last handshake message, it sends TLS application data 0x00 as a protected success indication. The peer replies with an empty EAP-Response, and the server then sends EAP-Success. Early data and post-handshake authentication MUST NOT be used, and implementations SHOULD NOT send KeyUpdate.

To allow resumption, the server MUST send one or more post-handshake NewSessionTicket messages after the initial authentication. TLS 1.3 limits ticket lifetime to 604800 seconds (7 days) and servers MUST respect that. A single ticket is usually enough. Resumption cuts round trips and lets the server skip database lookups. Peers are RECOMMENDED to resume with a valid unused ticket, and servers are RECOMMENDED to accept, but a server MAY demand a full handshake. Resumption SHOULD offer a key_share and use psk_dhe_ke so that forward secrecy is kept.

A HelloRetryRequest adds one extra round trip when the server needs different key share parameters. The RFC also shows a flow with no peer authentication, for example for emergency services.
sections.plainLanguage: You show your ID, the network shows its ID, and then it quietly says a secret word to prove everything worked. It can also hand you a short-lived pass so next time you skip most of the checking.

sections.title: Identity and Privacy
sections.content:
EAP-TLS 1.3 is always used with privacy. Cipher suites without confidentiality are forbidden, and TLS 1.3 encrypts the certificate messages, so the extra empty-certificate round used for privacy in earlier versions is not needed. The normal message flow already has privacy.

Peers and servers supporting TLS 1.3 MUST support anonymous Network Access Identifiers (NAIs). A client MUST NOT send its username or any other permanent identifier in cleartext in the Identity Response. The RECOMMENDED form omits the username (@realm); a fixed username such as anonymous@realm or an encrypted one is allowed. The NAI MUST be a UTF-8 string.

Some privacy still leaks. The realm in the NAI is typically visible, and without padding the sizes of EAP-TLS packets reveal the size of the client certificate. Peers SHOULD use TLS record padding. The RFC also warns that a peer willing to fall back to TLS 1.2 with static RSA key exchange and no privacy can be tricked by an active attacker into disclosing its username, so peers are RECOMMENDED not to do that.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like writing only the street name on an envelope instead of your full name. People can still see roughly where you are from, but not who you are.

sections.title: Verifying Who Is Who
sections.content:
The identity in EAP-Response/Identity is not authenticated by EAP-TLS. Unauthenticated information MUST NOT be used for accounting or to give authorization. The server MAY use it for routing and method selection, and MAY reject conversations that do not fit its policy.

The server's identity is normally a fully qualified domain name in the SubjectAltName (SAN) extension of its certificate. Peers SHOULD let users configure one or more trusted root certificates and one or more server names to match against the SAN. Without name matching, and with a public root CA, effectively any server could obtain a certificate that the peer trusts. Because configuring this is non-trivial, automated provisioning is RECOMMENDED; the RFC mentions the eduroam Configuration Assistant Tool as an example.

Where no trusted root is available, peers MAY use trust on first use (TOFU), storing the server certificate at the first connection. The RFC cautions that TOFU does not allow the server certificate to change without out-of-band validation and raises the risk of traffic interception. This section applies to EAP-TLS regardless of the TLS version.
sections.plainLanguage: The name you shout at the door is not proof of anything. The real proof is the ID card, and you should only trust ID cards from offices you already know.

sections.title: Key Derivation with the TLS Exporter
sections.content:
TLS 1.3 replaces the old pseudorandom function with HKDF and a completely new key schedule, so the key hierarchy in RFC 5216 no longer holds. Instead, the Key_Material and Method-Id are derived using the TLS exporter interface, with the EAP Type value 0x0D as context.

The Master Session Key (MSK) is the first 64 bytes of the key material and the Extended MSK (EMSK) is the next 64. The IV values RECV-IV and SEND-IV are not exported. The key derivation MUST use the exact lengths given. Truncating by asking the exporter for less output, which was possible in TLS 1.2, does not work in TLS 1.3. An implementation that wants only part of the output MUST ask for the full output and use the part it needs.

The RFC does not specify how lower layers use the MSK. It registers the two exporter labels with IANA, both marked as not usable with DTLS and recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides mix their secrets in a fixed recipe to bake the same secret keys. The recipe must be followed exactly, with the exact amounts, or the keys will not match.

sections.title: Failure, Termination and State Handling
sections.content:
In TLS 1.3 all error alerts are fatal, and the only warning-level alerts are close_notify and user_canceled. TLS 1.3 does not require sending an alert after a fatal error, but EAP-TLS 1.3 strengthens this: whenever an implementation hits a fatal error it MUST send an appropriate TLS Error alert. The RFC shows flows where the server rejects the ClientHello, where the peer rejects the server, and where the server rejects the peer; each ends with EAP-Failure.

For the state machines, a TLS Error alert SHOULD be treated as a failure result indication. After sending or receiving an alert, the server may only send an EAP-Failure. After it sends the protected success indication, the server must not send more EAP-Requests and may only send EAP-Success. It MUST NOT send the 0x00 record before it has processed the client Finished and sent its last handshake message.

Keying material can be derived once the server Finished has been sent or received, and made available to lower layers after the authenticated success indication.
sections.plainLanguage: If something goes wrong, you must say so out loud instead of silently walking away. And the network only says it is happy after everything has really been checked.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security claims of RFC 5216 stay the same but get stronger. TLS 1.3 only defines strong algorithms and EAP-TLS 1.3 always provides forward secrecy. Weak algorithms such as 3DES, CBC mode, RC4, SHA-1, MD5, P-192 and RSA-1024 have not been registered for use in TLS 1.3.

Revocation checking is mandatory. All certificates in the chain except the trust anchor MUST be checked. Servers MUST implement OCSP stapling, and peers that use it MUST treat a certificate entry without a valid status as invalid. Because the peer may have no connectivity before authentication, peers MUST also support checking revocation after authentication completes, and SHOULD NOT trust the network until they have done so.

Resumption must be based on cached data from the original handshake, and if that data cannot be retrieved securely, resumption MUST NOT be done. Peers MUST NOT keep tickets or PSKs longer than 604800 seconds (7 days). Because identity or other information can change between the first handshake and resumption (a time-of-check time-of-use problem), decisions MUST be reevaluated if the changed information could alter them. The RFC also recommends separate certificates and resumption caches for different protocols to avoid cross-protocol attacks.

Authorization and accounting MUST be based on authenticated information, such as the certificate, not on the unauthenticated identity. Implementations MUST mitigate known attacks on TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: The network must check that no ID card has been cancelled, and it must keep checking when you come back with a pass. Old passes expire after a week, and nobody gets extra powers just because they were let in before.

data.title: EAP-TLS 1.3 key material
data.code:
Type = 0x0D
Key_Material = TLS-Exporter("EXPORTER_EAP_TLS_Key_Material",
                            Type, 128)
Method-Id    = TLS-Exporter("EXPORTER_EAP_TLS_Method-Id",
                            Type, 64)
Session-Id   = Type || Method-Id

MSK          = Key_Material(0, 63)
EMSK         = Key_Material(64, 127)
